t: Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen
s: Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen Our first plan was a sealed growth chamber with hydroponics inside it. Arabidopsis needs steady humidity, temperature and light to give comparable results, and the school lab could not hold any of those steady. The chamber was meant to give us a controlled box to run every plant experiment in. This was the last week of design before we started buying parts. GROWTH CHAMBER · PRE-PIVOT · WEEK Felix, Noah, Audrey, Anton, Anna, Eva, Timmy, Chloe Finished the chamber layout and ran airflow studies on the enclosure. Fans, ducting and shelf spacing sized around a 3 tray capacity. Inspired by the Katagiri chamber (2015) research paper. Air circulation diagram Light distribution graph Built four sourcing lists, split by where we would actually buy each part. Electronics and control from Guanghua. Structure from Test Rite. Plants and water systems from the Jianguo flower market. Containers from IKEA. Fans, timers, DS18B20 temperature sensors, blackout cloth, a Mylar substitute, air pumps and air stones. Combined sourcing list 27 March, NTU plant lab visit: the hydroponic set-ups we were trying to copy inside the chamber Costed the whole build and took it to the instructors. The total was never written down in this record. Stopped on 28 March, told to buy nothing and print nothing. The instructors were still weighing the effort against the risk and against what the chamber would be worth to us later. Nothing had been ordered, so the freeze cost us planning time and nothing else. Freeze purchasing instead of building in parallel If half of it was already built we’d have argued to keep going. We hadn’t spent anything yet, so stopping was free. Ordering the slow-delivery parts anyway to keep the option open. Nobody had defended the chamber yet, so that would have been buying our way into a decision. We picked the chamber before checking it was the right build Wait for the instructors’ evaluation before any further design work, and agree a hardware budget before the next sourcing round. Read the new direction document when it lands. Brainstorm against it before defending the chamber.

t: Visiting Prof. Verslues
s: Visiting Prof. Verslues We had a chamber design nobody had agreed to and a purchasing freeze. None of us had seen a working plant growth setup, so we went to look at one before designing any more of our own. HUMIDITY BOX · ORIGIN · CONSULTATION Anton, Noah Visited Prof. Verslues’s lab at Academia Sinica on 3 April. Looked at how his incubator holds conditions across a whole tray at once. Trays sit on wire shelving with airflow coming from underneath. He grows at a much lower density than we had been planning for. Incubator shelf with vertical agar plates Photometer we saw at his lab that measures cell density Came back and dropped the full chamber in favour of a humidity box. Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up, and a box holding one tray is a build we could actually finish. Build a humidity box, not a growth chamber Small enough that we’d actually finish it. Humidity is the condition that decides whether the seeds come up. Carrying on with the full chamber. It was frozen anyway, and after seeing a real one we couldn’t justify the size. No target humidity range written down, and nothing to measure it with Get the range Arabidopsis needs, and put a sensor on the next electronics order. Design the box around a target humidity range, not around the space we happen to have.

t: Told to drop soil sensing
s: Told to drop soil sensing Our original plan was to sense drought stress in soil and release protectant into the soil directly. Before committing to it we wanted someone who sells into agriculture to tell us whether it held up. DIRECTION · PROF. CHEN · CONSULTATION Anton, Timmy, Jessie Met Prof. Chen (陳文亮) on 10 April. He has commercial products in the smart agriculture market we were aiming at. Meeting in progress Bioreactor start-up poster Prof. Chen pointed us to Were told to drop soil moisture sensing entirely. Cheap sensors already dominate that market and they are inaccurate. Calibrating a sensor across soil types takes three to four months of data for each one. Took his second point, that soil release is hard to defend on biosafety. Engineered bacteria going into open soil is a much harder case to make than bacteria kept inside a vessel. He pushed us toward containment. Reframed the business model around the consumable instead of the device. Sell the cartridge, not the box, the way printers and ink work. His idea, not ours. Drop soil sensing and move to a contained vessel A market already served by cheap sensors is not one we can enter with a school budget. Containment is easier to defend than release, and we were going to be asked about it. Soil calibration across types. Three to four months of data for each one, which we do not have. No bioreactor design exists yet Ask Dr. Pak for the reactor landscape before choosing a configuration. Soil compatibility now unclaimable If we ever claim it, it needs the 3–4 months of data per soil he described. Get the reactor families from Dr. Pak so the new direction has a shape.

t: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start
s: The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start This is the week the project changed shape. The pivot document went up on 15 April: instead of sensing soil and releasing into it, engineered B. subtilis would live inside a sealed vessel, and light would tell them when to produce protectant. That vessel is a bioreactor, and none of us had built one or knew where to start. BIOREACTOR · CONCEPT · CONSULTATION Anton, Noah, Timmy Posted the pivot on 15 April. Input soil stress, output green or red light into a contained chamber. Seven people reacted to the message. Every instrument in this notebook follows from it. The pivot as posted on 15 April: stress sensed, light switches the strains, protectant crosses a membrane 18 April: our first hardware sketch on the whiteboard Asked Dr. Pak, Dean of Research, for the reactor landscape. He set out five families. Continuous stirred tank, bubble column, air lift, fluidised bed, packed bed. He suggested a packed bed for our case, with bacteria immobilised in the column. Took his scoping advice, which mattered more than the recommendation itself. He said bioreactor design is an enormous field and there is no need to invent something new. Adapting a common design to our needs would itself be the achievement. We went on to choose hollow-fibre tangential flow, which is not what he suggested. That conversation happened in person and nobody wrote down why. Adapt an existing reactor design instead of inventing one Adapting an existing design became the goal, so the scope stopped growing. Five families to choose from instead of a blank page. Nothing yet. Hollow fibre was recommended in person and nobody wrote it down, so we can’t say why we didn’t take the packed-bed suggestion. No record of why hollow fibre over packed bed Ask Dr. Pak to put the reasoning in a message so it exists in writing. No selection criteria were written down Write the criteria out now and mark them as reconstructed. Specify a hollow-fibre configuration we can actually buy in Taipei.

t: Working out what a stress assay should measure
s: Working out what a stress assay should measure The pivot had landed but the plant side of the project had no experiment behind it. Before building anything for the plants we needed to agree what stress we would apply, at what level, and what we would measure to say whether the protectant worked. HYDROPONICS · ASSAY STANDARD · WEEK Anton, Noah Argued out what a standard stress assay would look like for us. Salinity came up more than heat, mostly because it is easier to apply consistently. Sketched the hollow-fibre loop and printed the first hydroponic plate. The whiteboard sketch is the first drawing of a membrane module in our record. The plate is a flat holder with seed holes, before any idea of floating it. 25 April: hollow-fibre membrane loop sketched on the whiteboard 26 April: first printed hydroponic plates No agreed stress assay Pick the stress, the concentration and the readout, and write them down. Set milestones and deadlines per task so the quiet weeks are visible in advance.

t: Nothing much happened
s: Nothing much happened A quiet week. Several of us were away and nothing moved on the hardware. Kept in the record because a notebook containing only the productive weeks misrepresents how the summer actually went. LOW ACTIVITY WEEK · WEEK Anton No photographs, messages or files on the hardware side are dated to this week. A week lost with nothing scheduled Agree deadlines per task so gaps are planned instead of discovered. Milestones per task, requested by the instructors.

t: Four instruments, three people
s: Four instruments, three people The instructors asked for a milestone and a deadline against every task in the project. Writing the list turned out to be more useful than the list itself. MILESTONES · WEEK Anton, Noah, Timmy Listed every task in progress with an owner and a date. Two tasks had no owner at all until the list was written. Found we had four instruments in progress and three people to lead them. Humidity box, imaging station, light plate, fluorometer, with the bioreactor about to start. Left the fluorometer decision to the following week. Nothing was built this week. The output was an uncomfortable conclusion. 9 May: the hydroponic prototype set up for the wet lab, the one piece of hardware that moved Four instruments, not enough people Drop one. Decide which next week. Decide on the fluorometer.

t: Dropping the fluorometer
s: Dropping the fluorometer The chlorophyll fluorometer would have let us measure plant stress directly, by reading damage to photosystem II. Fv/Fm is the standard number for that, and a healthy plant sits around 0.78 to 0.83. It was the fourth instrument we had in progress and there were three of us. FLUOROMETER · PHOTOMETER · WEEK Timmy, Anton, Eva Made the case for building it. It measures the outcome the project claims to improve, so it would test our own claim directly. Commercial meters run past NT$100,000 and the open-source Open-JIP design already exists, so the gap looked worth closing. The Open-JIP layout we evaluated (published figure, shared in #dry-fluorometer on 9 April) 13 May: checking agar plants by eye, the measurement a fluorometer would have replaced Dropped it on 11 May, on capacity, not feasibility. Anton moved to the bioreactor. Eva took a different task. The Open-JIP evaluation was never written up, so anyone picking it up starts from nothing. Wrote the photometer requirement on 16 May, in nine words. We need to measure flow rate, and how much B. subtilis there is. The shape of the answer followed immediately: flow cuvette plus spectrometer, 600 nm beam, a sensor reading light decay, an intensity controller. 16 May: bioreactor layout A sketched the same day 16 May: layout B Drop the fluorometer on capacity, not feasibility The science holds up. It was never a feasibility problem, only a staffing one. Better to finish two instruments than half-finish three. Building it anyway with a part-time lead. Three half-finished instruments is worse than two finished and one we admit we skipped. No direct measure of plant stress response Either source a commercial meter for final validation, or state the gap on the wiki. Open-JIP evaluation never written up Write it up anyway so a future team can start from it. Specify the photometer optics. Flow cuvette, beam path, and what the sensor actually reads.

t: Humidity box finished, agar photos useless
s: Humidity box finished, agar photos useless The humidity box is a small sealed enclosure that keeps humidity steady while Arabidopsis germinates. It came out of the Verslues visit and it is the first thing we finished. The same week we started growing on agar plates, and ran into a problem we had not planned for. HUMIDITY BOX · IMAGING STATION · BUILD Anton, Noah Finished the humidity box and put the first seeds in. We have no log of what humidity and temperature it actually holds. Started photographing agar plates to track germination. The photos were useless. The angle moved between shots, the room light changed with the time of day, and the shadows moved with it. Two plates photographed on different days told us nothing about how much had grown. Spent two afternoons shooting a transparent dish on a white table, trying to find a repeatable setup by hand. It did not work, but it told us what was moving: angle, distance, background and ambient light. A fix has to hold all four at once, which a person with a phone cannot do. Bought the first round of electronics at Guanghua on 21 May. LEDs, breadboards, jumpers and an Arduino for the light plate and the imaging station. 21 May: the electronics run at Guanghua market Split ownership. Anton took the light plate, Noah took the bioreactor. Both of us kept working on the other one. Build a station instead of writing a procedure A written procedure still depends on whoever is holding the phone. If the geometry is locked in plastic, the photos come out comparable whether you’re careful or not. A tripod and a taped mark on the bench. Cheaper, does nothing about room light, and it’s wrong the moment someone moves the tripod. Humidity box has no recorded target range Log the humidity and temperature it actually holds, and over what period. No way yet to compare plates across days Build the station. Lock the phone, the light and the background. Design and build the imaging station around the four variables the hand tests exposed.

t: Building the agar plate imaging station
s: Building the agar plate imaging station The imaging station is a rig that holds a phone in a fixed position over an agar plate, under fixed lighting, so photos taken days apart can be compared. It is the answer to the problem from last week. IMAGING STATION · BUILD Anton, Noah Built a four-legged frame with a slot at the top for the phone. The phone contacts the corner and locks, which fixes position and angle with no moving parts. The light ring lit inside the station 31 May: phone seated over a plate in the station CAD of the frame and phone slot Added a dark lid so no room light reaches the plate, and an LED ring inside as the only light source. Worked out the light ring, which was the hard part. We wanted the light in a circle and angled in toward the plate. Bending an LED strip into an angled circle makes it twist and compress along its length at once, and it buckles somewhere unpredictable. Putting ridges around the ring fixed it. The strip creases at each ridge, the tension goes out, and the creases land where we chose. Cut a slot with two guide rails so the strip slides in instead of being glued down. A dead LED can be replaced without reprinting the ring, which takes six hours. Made the white bottom plate removable from underneath on four screws. Swap it for black and the photo background changes with no reprint. Every part of the station comes apart the same way. 1 June: first use of the station Checking the frame before the first plate Wiring the LED ring Ridges to take the tension out, and a slide-in slot Creasing at the ridges is predictable. Left alone the strip buckles wherever it wants. With a slot we can replace the strip without reprinting the ring. Gluing the strip onto a smooth angled ring. It works against the strip, and replacing an LED would mean reprinting the part. Lighting evenness across the plate never measured Photograph a blank plate and check for a brightness gradient across the frame. No fixed camera settings recorded Lock exposure and white balance, and write the settings into the protocol. Use it on the real salinity plates and find out whether day-to-day comparison holds up.

t: Assembly guide tested by handing it over
s: Assembly guide tested by handing it over The light plate apparatus (LPA, called DiOPAL until October) shines green and red light into wells of bacteria. Green switches the CcaS-CcaR circuit on and red switches it off, so the plate is how we control when the bacteria produce. Prototype 1 only had to prove we could light 24 wells evenly. LIGHT PLATE · LPA-1 · BUILD Noah, Anton, Chloe, Sophie Seated the 24-well printed plate and wired the Arduino and breadboard to the first row. Nothing is soldered. It is all breadboard and jumper leads. 27 May: 24-well plate mid-assembly LED harness in the first row Plate wired to the breadboard Wrote the assembly guide to step level, each step small enough to stop between. LPA_Assembly_Guide_v2.docx. Stopped at step 15 on purpose and left a note to continue from step 16. The next person picked it up from the document alone with no verbal handoff. It is the only check we have that the guide is good enough for someone else to build from. 28 May: troubleshooting the assembly from the guide 30 May: plate handed over mid-build 30 May: working through the guide with our advisor Neo Left the lid unfixed and wrote it down. It needs filing on the long axis and the school closed on us. Cosmetic for prototype 1, and the lid geometry changes at prototype 2 anyway. TABLE 8 Parts as actually fitted. The lid fault is recorded here instead of being left to the photographs. Plate 24-well, 3D printed lid does not seat LEDs 520 nm green, 660 nm red first row only MCU Arduino Uno breadboarded, not soldered Guide LPA_Assembly_Guide_v2.docx step level, 20+ steps On the same bench, the photometer lit for the first time on 28 May. Two wet-lab members wired the amber LED after school. The whiteboard design it follows went up the day before. 27 May: photometer optics on the whiteboard 28 May: photometer first light, wired by the wet lab 31 May: plate at the end of the week Leave the lid and write it down It does not block the 13 June date, and that is the only date that matters this month. The geometry changes at prototype 2, so any fix now gets thrown away. Reprinting at a looser tolerance. Nine hours of print time against five minutes with a file. Well-to-well output never measured Lux meter at each of the 24 wells at fixed height, one pass per channel. Lid does not seat File the long axis, then measure what came off so prototype 2 starts there. Nothing soldered yet, it is all breadboard Solder the harness once the well spacing is final. Measure homogeneity. It is the stated acceptance criterion and we have not checked it once.

t: Bioreactor prototype I built
s: Bioreactor prototype I built The bioreactor is the vessel the pivot committed us to. Bacteria live inside a hollow fibre membrane while the protectant they make crosses the membrane and leaves, which keeps the organism contained. Prototype I is the simplest version of that we could build. BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I · BUILD Anton, Noah, Joshua, Chars Built prototype I on 6 June from four parts. PES hollow fibre membrane with around 200 mL of lumen volume, a 500 mL reservoir holding 300 mL of LB, a peristaltic pump, and a luer valve on the loop for sampling. 6 June: prototype I on the bench, culture going in Prototype I as designed: membrane, pump, sampling valve, reservoir Inoculated with 20 mL of a multi-overnight B. subtilis culture. Deliberately left everything else off. No stirring, no aeration, no pH control. We did not know which of those we needed. Starting with none means every addition later has a reason behind it we can point at. Adding them all at once would have meant several things failing together with no way to tell which mattered. Drove both light plate wavelengths for the first time, green 520 nm and red 660 nm. First row of wells only, driven independently. Green is the on command for the CcaS-CcaR circuit and red is the off command. 1 June: light plate, first light in both colours Built the round vertical agar stand. TABLE 9 Prototype I as built on 6 June. Simple continuous flow-through, nothing active in the reservoir. Membrane PES hollow fibre lumen ~200 mL Reservoir 500 mL bottle, 300 mL LB no stirring Pump peristaltic target 94 mL/min Sampling luer valve on the loop, not the reservoir Build the simplest loop we can Each thing we add later then has a reason behind it we can point at. It also means the first run tells us something even if it fails. Building it fully specified from the start. More parts failing together, and no way to attribute anything. No active mixing, and the sampling port is on the loop, not the reservoir Add a stirrer if growth is poor, and move the port to the reservoir outlet where there is more volume. No temperature control on the loop Decide whether we run at room temperature or in the incubator, and keep it the same between runs. Run it and get a growth curve against a flask control.

t: The cells barely grow in the reactor
s: The cells barely grow in the reactor This is the first run of prototype I. We grew the same culture in the reactor and in a flask at the same time, both at room temperature, so the flask acts as a control. If the reactor works, the two curves should look alike. BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE I · FAILURE DIAGNOSIS Gabriel, Abby, Anton, Noah Paired growth curves against a flask control at room temperature. The flask climbed past 2.4 over 25 hours. The reactor stayed almost flat and ended near 0.3, and the run terminated early on a leak at the pump. Sampled both arms every thirty minutes for eight hours, then again at 25 hours. One person had to stay with it for the whole run. Prototype I loop on the bench: pump, membrane cartridge, reservoir OD600 against time: flask (blue) to ~2.4, reactor (orange) flat near 0.3 Got a flask that climbed past 2.4 and a reactor that stayed almost flat near 0.3. The numbers inside the system disagreed too, 0.304 in the tube against 0.48 in the reservoir. That should not happen if the loop is mixed. Terminated early when medium leaked at the peristaltic pump. The leak was at the pump head, where the tubing flexes most. Plated 2 mL from the shell side of the membrane on LB and got no colonies at all. That is our evidence the membrane holds the bacteria in. It came out of the run that otherwise failed. Shell-side plate, no colonies 13 June: the loop redrawn for prototype II after this run CANDIDATE CAUSES · TABLE 10 Ruled out means we ran the test. To test means we have not. No active mixing, cells settle Add a stirrer and repeat. to test Nutrient stratification Same test as above. to test Room temperature too low Run the next attempt at 37 °C. to test Sampling port unrepresentative Move the port to the reservoir outlet. to fix Change three things at once and accept we will not know which worked Stirring, temperature and sampling position are all cheap to change and all plausible. We have weeks, not months. We couldn’t afford to change one thing at a time. Testing one variable at a time. That’s the right way to do it and we chose speed instead. Writing it down here so nobody reads prototype II as proof that stirring alone fixed it. Three variables change together in prototype II Any of the three could be the real cause. Say that, instead of claiming stirring fixed it. Leak at the peristaltic pump Upgrade to BPT tubing before the next run. Prototype II. Magnetic stirring at 200 rpm, sampling moved to the reservoir outlet, run at 37 °C.

t: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours
s: Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours Prototype I barely grew and we had four candidate reasons. Prototype II changes three of them at once, which is not how you isolate a cause, but we had weeks, not months. BIOREACTOR · PROTOTYPE II · TEST Gabriel, Abby, Anton, Noah Added a 200 rpm magnetic stirrer to the reservoir to stop cells settling out. The stirrer bar was the largest one we had, which may be part of why it worked so well. Moved the sampling port to the reservoir outlet, where there is far more volume. A sample from there represents the whole system, not one length of tube. Ran both arms at 37 °C instead of room temperature, pump held at 94 mL/min. 14 June: sampling the reactor arm Sampling the flask arm Prototype II: stirrer under the reservoir, sampler beside it The sampling procedure, written out by hand for whoever took the next shift Page 2 of the procedure OD600 against minutes at 37 °C: reactor (orange) and flask (blue) Got a full growth curve, and the reactor beat its own flask control. Reactor plateaued at OD600 0.8 to 0.9 after two hours. Flask reached 0.6 to 0.8 after four and a half. TABLE 11 Full growth curve secured. The reactor reached plateau faster and higher than the flask. Bioreactor 0.8 – 0.9 2 h flat at ~0.3 Flask control 0.6 – 0.8 4.5 h reached 2.4 at 25 h The DBTL summary slide we made for prototype II Passed. Faster to plateau and higher than the control Faster to plateau and higher at plateau than the control, which is more than we expected. Whether stirring alone would have done it, we cannot say. Claiming stirring fixed it. Three variables moved and only one of them is in the headline. Three changes at once, so we cannot say which one did it Run stirring alone at 22 °C, which also gets us the temperature we would actually operate at. Evaluate at 22 °C, and upgrade to BPT tubing to stop the degradation seen in earlier trials.

t: Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design
s: Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design Prof. Chang (張嘉修) is a chair professor in chemical engineering at NCKU who has published on B. subtilis bioreactor systems, so he was the right person to show the design to. He found a hole in it that none of us had seen. BIOREACTOR · PROF. CHANG · CONSULTATION Anton, Noah, Timmy Showed him the design in person on 18 June. He spent longer on containment than on the biology, which we had not expected. 18 June: presenting the design Prof. Chang’s feedback Discussing the membrane Were told the hollow fibre and the light module are the parts that make the project distinctive. But we need to be able to explain to a judge why hollow fibre specifically, and we could not. Took the main criticism. We had no mechanism at all for getting protectant out of the membrane. His suggestion was a valve after the membrane, to build pressure and push the permeate through. Posted a stepper pinch valve design to the build channel the next day, with a 27 June target. There was no valve on any plan before we spoke to him. 19 June: the stepper pinch valve design posted with a 27 June target Flow against cam position at 5, 10 and 15 psi, posted with the valve design 15 June: the ‘ultimate design’ drawn before the meeting, with no valve after the membrane Logged three things he raised that we have still done nothing about. Foaming from B. subtilis surfactant, which he mentioned twice. Resting cells. The cartridge format. Group photo after the meeting 17 June: the roadmap redrawn around his points Add a valve after the membrane A valve after the membrane is the mechanism we were missing entirely. Hydroponics as the delivery target, which also narrows the biosafety case. Membrane sizing becomes a design variable, no longer a fixed part. Resting cells, and the cartridge format. Raised in the meeting, no design response yet. Foaming not addressed Raised twice, no response. Add a foam trap or say why we didn’t. Lux to PPFD conversion never recorded Write down the factor we used and where it came from. Every light dose we quote rests on it. Post the pinch valve design and set a print date. Chang’s other points still need answers.

t: Wrong unit for the light dose
s: Wrong unit for the light dose The CcaS-CcaR circuit responds to a specific photon flux, so the light dose the plate delivers has to be a known quantity. This week we found we had been about to measure it in entirely the wrong unit. LIGHT PLATE · DOSE UNITS · TEST Anton, Noah, Timmy Checked the Castillo-Hair paper and found its half-maximal point is 4.66 µmol per square metre per second. That is a photon flux density. It counts photons. Checked what our meters read, and found every affordable one reads illuminance in lux. Lux is weighted for human vision, which peaks around 555 nm. Our green sits at 520 and our red at 660, both well off that peak. So the conversion error is not even the same size on the two channels. Bought a lux meter and set out to derive the conversion for our own LED spectra. A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget. A phone app was considered and rejected as not repeatable between handsets. Caught it before any dose figure went out, so nothing published needs correcting. The factor we actually used is not written down anywhere. TABLE 12a The two units measure different things and cannot be converted without knowing the spectrum. CcaS–CcaR half-maximal 4.66 ± 0.63 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ Castillo-Hair 2019 Hill coefficient 1.88 ± 0.16 — same t½ ON / OFF 105.1 / 74.97 min same What our meter reads — lux — Conversion factor we used — — never written down The light plate apparatus we were following, shown with its photon-flux spectra (published figure, shared on 24 June) Buy a lux meter and derive the conversion ourselves A proper PPFD sensor was out of budget and we needed a number that week. Quoting the paper’s number in lux and hoping. Every dose we published afterwards would have been wrong by a factor nobody could reproduce. The conversion factor we used is not written down anywhere Find it, write it down with the spectrum assumption, and restate every dose figure in PPFD. Green and red need different factors Compute both from the LED spectra, not one number for the plate. Write the factor down. Until it exists, no light dose in this project is reproducible.

t: Temperature sensor driving the green channel
s: Temperature sensor driving the green channel The whole project is one sentence: sense stress, emit light, release protectant. This is the first time the sensing end and the light end ran together on a bench, two months after the pivot. STRESS TO LIGHT · FIRMWARE · BUILD Anton, Noah, Neo Wired an SHT31 temperature and humidity sensor to the Arduino over I2C. It reports humidity too, which the code reads and then ignores. Wrote a linear stress fraction between a floor and a ceiling temperature. Below 32 °C the LED is off. At 50 °C and above it is at full brightness. Between those it scales linearly. Mapped the fraction onto a PWM green channel and ran it. The transfer function is four lines of code, deliberately. Anything more shaped would be invented, since we have no data on how stress response scales with temperature. 20 June: bench session with our advisor Neo, the week the demo ran Wrote it up as Stress_to_Light_Demo_Manual.docx. 32 °C and 50 °C are guesses, not measurements. Only the green channel is driven, so the demo switches the circuit on but not off. TABLE 12b Four constants and a straight line between two of them. TEMP_BASE 32.0 °C below this the LED is off TEMP_MAX 50.0 °C at or above this, full brightness Between linear stress fraction 0 to 1 drives PWM duty Sensor SHT31 temperature and humidity, I2C Linear between two thresholds, nothing more shaped Two thresholds are easy to change once the wet lab gives us real numbers. Anything more shaped would be a guess dressed up as a model. A sigmoid or a lookup table. Neither is supported by anything we measured. TEMP_BASE and TEMP_MAX are guesses Get the real heat-stress thresholds for Arabidopsis from the wet lab and replace them. Red channel not in the loop Add the OFF command so the demo shows both directions, not just on. Humidity is read but not used The SHT31 gives it for free. Decide whether it should feed the stress fraction. Replace the placeholder thresholds with numbers from the wet lab.

t: Making the plate float
s: Making the plate float Arabidopsis grows hydroponically on a plate sitting over liquid medium. The roots have to reach the liquid without the plate flooding, and our first version was fixed in place, which meant setting the level by hand every day and getting it wrong. HYDROPONICS · FLOATING PLATE · BUILD Anton Built a fixed plate with a liquid chamber underneath, and found the level impossible to hold. It has to sit as high as possible without coming over the growing platform, and it drops as the plants drink, so the roots end up in air. 13 June: the fixed-plate hydroponic box in use 25 June: first floating plate, washer poles at the corners Redesigned it to float on the medium instead. The frame of the platform is built as sealed air chambers, so it rides on the surface and stays at the same height above the liquid whatever the level does. Calculated the buoyancy before printing, not by tuning it afterwards. A hollow frame cannot be adjusted once printed, so print orientation and wall thickness now decide whether it floats. Added poles at the corners to take washers as weights. Adding weight is easier than adding volume, so the poles are the margin for error. The washers we have are heavier than the calculation wanted, so the adjustment is coarse. Printed the first iteration on 25 June. A later iteration (Prototype 3, undated in our record) shrank the footprint, added clip-in handles and dropped the poles once the chamber volume was tuned. Prototype 3 in CAD, cut through the seed holders: sealed chambers in violet Prototype 3 printed parts: plate, two clip-in handles, thirteen seed holders Float the platform instead of controlling the level The height stays correct as the medium level drops. A level sensor and a top-up pump. More parts, more to break, and it solves something the shape solves for nothing. Buoyancy not verified with plants on it, and the weight poles may be unnecessary Float it fully loaded, measure the freeboard, and see whether the washers are needed at all. Print it, float it, and find out how far off the maths was.

t: Iteration 1. Bubbles and drift
s: Iteration 1. Bubbles and drift The photometer measures how much B. subtilis is in the reactor loop without taking samples out. An amber LED shines through a thin flow cuvette and we read how much light gets through. A beamsplitter sends part of the beam to a reference sensor first, so drift in the LED shows up in both channels and divides out. (The wiki numbers the bench layout as Prototype 1, so this iteration is its Prototype 2.) PHOTOMETER · ITERATION 1 · BUILD Anton, Noah, Joshua Printed a rail where the LED, lens, beamsplitter, cuvette holder and both sensors each position independently. None of us knew where the components should sit, so we made all of them movable and worked it out on the bench. Before the rail: optics in magnetic clamps, spacings taken with a caliper Iteration 1 on its printed rail 2 July: lens and beam line visible Ran the beam horizontally through the flow cuvette and plumbed it into the loop. Got data that fluctuated far too much to use, for two reasons that made each other worse. Bubbles formed inside the cuvette and sat in the beam. A bubble moves the reading in a step, not as noise around it. The lens and beamsplitter mounts were loose enough that the alignment drifted while we watched it. LED lit through the cuvette Instructor setting up the trial with us Iteration 1 at work Decided to move the cuvette down to the base for the next build. Bubbles rise, so putting the cuvette at the bottom takes them out of the beam without us doing anything. A dual luer valve and syringes let us pull gas out on demand. Move the cuvette to the base Bubbles rise, so putting the cuvette at the bottom takes them out of the beam without us doing anything. A dual luer valve and syringes let us pull the gas out on demand. Mounting vertically at the same time, since the geometry has to change anyway. A fixed rail with no adjustment. More stable, but no way to find the alignment. Bubbles in the flow cuvette Move the cuvette to the base and add a dual luer valve and syringes to bleed the gas. Loose lens and beamsplitter tolerances Tighten the mounts on the next iteration. Rebuild with the cuvette low, tighter tolerances and a way to get the bubbles out.

t: Iteration 2. Zeroed against the wrong thing
s: Iteration 2. Zeroed against the wrong thing Iteration 1 drifted and bubbled. Iteration 2 moves the cuvette to the base, turns the whole assembly upright and tightens every mount. This is the first time we tested against a sample where we already knew the answer. PHOTOMETER · ITERATION 2 · TEST Anton, Noah, Joshua Rebuilt with the cuvette at the base, mounted vertically, tolerances tightened. Iteration 2 mounted vertically 4 July: amber beam visible through the box TiO₂ in the flow cuvette Blanked, then read medium alone, then medium with 2 mL of titanium dioxide as a known turbid sample. The titanium dioxide settles within a couple of minutes, so readings have to be taken promptly after mixing. Got 62.5 au against a true value of 0.75. The reference channel held steady at 92.5 lux across both readings, so that part of the design is behaving. Traced it to the blank, not the optics. Every reading after a bad blank carries that error, however good the hardware is. TABLE 15 True value for the TiO₂ sample is 0.75 au. Noted later (wiki, part 4.3): the firmware then divided the absorbance, 0.125, by the path entered in metres, which is where 62.5 comes from. On a 1 cm path the same reading is 0.62. Blank — — 0 Medium 660 lux 92.5 lux 0 au 2 mL TiO₂ 495 lux 92.5 lux 62.5 au Blank and sample side by side Reading taken in the dark room 4 July: the to-do board after the test Did not pass. The procedure was wrong, not the optics We zeroed against the medium instead of clear water, so the zero was wrong from the start. Everything after a bad blank carries that error, no matter how good the optics are. One reading against one known sample. It tells us the zero was wrong. It doesn’t tell us the instrument is linear. Blank taken on medium instead of clear water Reblank on distilled water and run the same TiO₂ readings again. Component tolerances still loose Decrease tolerances on the next build. Fix the procedure. Blank on clear water, tighten the tolerances, and run a dilution series.

t: Rewriting the spec, and pulling a claim
s: Rewriting the spec, and pulling a claim Bioreactor parts had been discussed across four Discord channels and several documents, and the numbers had drifted apart from each other. This week we wrote one specification and checked every line of it against the parts we had actually bought. BIOREACTOR · SPEC FREEZE · DECISION Anton, Noah, Timmy Wrote a single spec and marked what each line supersedes. Part numbers came off the invoices, not off the parts, so they should still be checked against what is fitted. Corrected the microcontroller and the membrane to what we own. ESP32 with a 12-bit ADC became Arduino Uno R4 with 14-bit. The membrane record became 0.2 µm, 150 cm², eight fibres. Withdrew our own biosafety claim. The old spec claimed a 50 kDa molecular weight cut-off and said the membrane blocks outer membrane vesicles. Neither is true of the part we bought. A 0.2 µm pore passes ACCD at around 36 kDa, which is what we want, but it also passes small vesicles and cell debris. Kept the one containment claim that still stands. The membrane does block whole B. subtilis. The shell-side plate in prototype I showed that. TABLE 15a Rows 3 and 4 withdraw a claim we had made. MCU Arduino Uno R4, 14-bit ADC ESP32, 12-bit board actually bought TFF module 0.2 µm, 150 cm², 8 fibres M+, 200 cm², 11 fibres module actually bought Pore claim 0.2 µm microfiltration 50 kDa MWCO wrong. retracted OMV blocking not claimed claimed 0.2 µm passes small OMVs Pressure sensor BP8G-AGA, 0–5 V — needs divider for the R4 Retract the containment claim instead of restating it quietly The pore we bought passes small vesicles and debris, so the old wording claimed more containment than we have. Leaving the old numbers in, once we had checked them against the datasheet. Containment now rests on cell size alone Say exactly what the membrane does and does not stop, on the wiki, in those words. Decide whether a second containment stage is needed now that the first claim is narrower.

t: Iteration 3. Response does not double
s: Iteration 3. Response does not double Iteration 2 was zeroed against the wrong reference, so its numbers meant nothing. Iteration 3 fixes the procedure, tilts the stand so bubbles clear, and this time reads two concentrations instead of one so we can see whether the response scales. PHOTOMETER · ITERATION 3 · TEST Anton, Noah, Joshua Built iteration 3 with tighter tolerances and a tilted stand. Iteration 3 on its tilted wedge 9 July: the column on its square stand Side view, Luer valve and syringes for bleeding gas Blanked on clear water this time, not on medium. That gives a zero we can defend. Read medium, then 1 mL of titanium dioxide, then 2 mL. Medium reads zero. 1 mL gives 0.3712 au. 2 mL gives 0.5785. Doubling the concentration gave 1.56 times the OD, not twice it. Either that is real Beer-Lambert behaviour at this path length or our transform is wrong, and two points cannot tell us which. Noticed two things we cannot explain. Absolute light dropped hard between builds, 660 lux down to 137. Something changed in the LED drive or the optics and we did not write down which. The reference moved from 17.23 to 18.33 between readings minutes apart. A reference should not do that. TABLE 16 Two concentrations instead of one. Doubling the TiO₂ moved OD from 0.3712 to 0.5785, not to 0.7424. Medium 137.63 lux 17.23 lux 0 au 1 mL TiO₂ 120.44 lux 18.33 lux 0.3712 au 2 mL TiO₂ 111.62 lux 18.33 lux 0.5785 au Wiring at the sensor end Procedure fixed, but the response does not scale Blanking on water gives us a zero we can defend. Absolute lux dropped hard between iterations, 660 to 137. Something changed in the LED drive or the optics and we didn’t write down which. Response is not proportional to concentration Run a five-point dilution series from 0.05 to 1.0 OD and plot it. Reference channel drifted between two readings minutes apart Log the reference on its own for an hour with nothing else changing. Build iteration 4 with the positions locked, then put it on the reactor.

t: Transmembrane pressure on a screen
s: Transmembrane pressure on a screen A hollow fibre membrane fouls as it runs, and fouling shows up as pressure building across the membrane. Until this week we had no way of seeing that happen, so we could not tell a clean run from a blocked one. BIOREACTOR · PRESSURE · BUILD Chars, Noah, Anton Fitted a BP8G-AGA pressure transducer on the retentate side. It reads 0 to 1 MPa and outputs 0 to 5 V. The board input is 0 to 3.3 V, so the divider is not optional. The divider is on a breadboard, not soldered, so the reading is only as steady as that joint. 10 July: transducer and Luer line before fitting 12 July: transmembrane pressure live on the laptop for the first time Had transmembrane pressure on a screen by the evening of 12 July. Logged but never zeroed against atmosphere, so the absolute values are suspect even though the shape is not. We can monitor the transmembrane pressure now. All we need is pinch valve and B. subtilis. Posted the trace and had the sawtooth on it explained the same day. Dr. Pak looked at the photograph and asked in one line whether the pulses were the peristaltic pump. They were. The exchange is in the channel, so we can account for the oscillation. Instrumented before fitting the pinch valve, even though the valve was designed and waiting. A valve on a loop we cannot measure tells us nothing, and pressure is what the valve controls. Instrument the loop before fitting the valve Put a valve on a loop we can’t measure and we won’t see what it does. Pressure is what the valve is there to control. Fitting the pinch valve first, which was already designed and waiting. Ordering it that way would have made the valve’s effect invisible. No pinch valve yet, so pressure cannot be controlled Print the valve and fit it after the membrane. Sawtooth amplitude never quantified Measure it peak to peak and check against the pump head rate. Fit the valve. Start the long photometer run on the reactor.

t: LPA V3 finished
s: LPA V3 finished Prototype 1 of the light plate lit one row back on 1 June. Milestone 2 asked for tunable intensity in both colours across the whole array. This is the packaged version, V3. LIGHT PLATE · LPA V3 · BUILD Anton, Noah, Joshua, Neo Packaged the array into a white well block on a black base, four rows by six columns. Twenty-four wells, which is more than any experiment we currently have planned needs. 17 July: printed parts arrived, first full assembly From above with tubes in, both colours On the base, side on Paired the columns into high, mid and low intensity groups, alternating green and red within each pair. Added a printed light-blocking shroud with a front slider. The array can be opened without unmounting it. The slider rattles slightly when open, which affects nothing. Drove all channels from the Arduino over PWM on separate pins. The intensity tiers are set by the wiring as well as the code, because we measured every LED and rewired them by brightness. The tiers hold even if the firmware changes. 11 July: the LED holder lit before packaging, tagged leads behind Front view: two LEDs not lighting Fixing the dead pair Sort the LEDs by hand instead of correcting in firmware LEDs that are supposed to be identical varied enough that PWM alone wouldn’t have kept the tiers apart. Sorting once is permanent. Correcting each LED in firmware would need redoing whenever one is replaced. Driving them all at the same duty and living with the spread. HIGH, MID and LOW would have overlapped. Still no measurement of what reaches each well, and it has never driven a real CcaS–CcaR experiment Lux meter at every well at fixed height, then run the optogenetic switch on it. Run a real optogenetic experiment on it. So far we’ve only checked the light.

t: Measuring every LED before wiring
s: Measuring every LED before wiring The intensity tiers on the light plate only mean something if the LEDs inside a tier actually match each other. Before wiring V3 we measured every LED we had bought, one at a time. LIGHT PLATE · LED CALIBRATION · TEST Anton, Noah Measured all 20 green and all 20 red LEDs at 5 V with a lux meter. Two of the reds were dead out of the packet and are not in the counts. Threw the first round of readings away. Moving the sensor around the structure changed the reading so much that the numbers were not comparable to each other. Printed a jig to hold the sensor at a fixed position and did the whole thing again. The jig fixes height but not angle, so there is still some error we have not quantified. The printed jig: one LED lit at the centre, lux meter behind 9 July: LEDs tagged by row and column 11 July: the full row of tagged LEDs Found more than 25 percent spread across parts sold as identical. Greens ranged 2.01 to 2.54 kLux. Reds ranged 360 to 438 lux. Tagged each LED by row and column, sorted them into matched sets of four, and rewired the array. After sorting, the low green tier spans 2.33 to 2.34 and the low red spans 0.390 to 0.397. We measured green in kLux and red in lux, which we should have caught before writing the table. TABLE 19 Matched sets after sorting. Greens in kLux, reds converted to kLux here from the lux readings. Low 2.33 – 2.34 0.390 – 0.397 green 0.01, red 0.007 Mid 2.35 – 2.37 0.410 – 0.416 green 0.02, red 0.006 High 2.38 – 2.50 0.424 – 0.431 green 0.12, red 0.007 Sorting into matched sets The sorted LEDs laid out before rewiring Passed. Matched sets hold the tiers apart Spread inside each tier after sorting is much smaller than the spread we started with. We characterised the LEDs, not the wells. What reaches each well is still unmeasured. Green and red are on different scales Green is in kLux and red is in lux. Pick one and redo the table. Recalibrated match targets left blank in the doc Fill in the target lux we recalibrated to, for green and for red. Measure light at the wells, not at the LEDs. That’s the acceptance criterion still open from May.

t: Reading four times high on the reactor
s: Reading four times high on the reactor Iteration 4 is the final photometer build, with the component positions fixed, TPU-lined mounts so the glass is not scratched, and snap-in covers along the light path to block room light. This is the first time it went onto the reactor and got read against a benchtop instrument on the same culture. PHOTOMETER · ON THE REACTOR · TEST Chars, Joshua, Noah, Anton Fitted it in line on the TFF loop and took a reading against the benchtop BioDrop. The BioDrop needs 2 mL per reading, which is a lot to take out of a running loop. 19 July: photometer in line on the loop, live data on the laptop The benchtop BioDrop reading 0.150 Calibrating the light sensor on the black body Inline spectrophotometer finally works and is able to measure the reasonable reading! … Looks like it overestimates around 4-fold. Got a first reading roughly four times high. That is an offset, not drift. A loose rail drifts, so we knew it was not the rail. Used Developer Mode to see both raw channels and rule them out. It holds the LED on and streams the raw sample and reference values. Both read cleanly, which left the blank as the only term they share. It was written to debug this and stayed as a permanent feature. Found the flow cuvette cannot be cleaned while it is inline, so the blank was taken through a dirty window. Joshua suggested typing the blank in by hand instead of measuring it. Chars patched that the same evening. The dashboard trace of the first in-line reading Close-up of the concave lens Iteration 4 assembled with its covers Re-read the same culture and got 0.100 against the BioDrop 0.149. The target agreed beforehand was 10 percent. We are 33 percent low, and the correction overshoots the other way. This is the second blanking failure on this instrument. Iteration 2 blanked on medium, this one blanked through a dirty cuvette. TABLE 20 Rows 3 and 4 are blank because the repeats were never run. The before-patch value was never written down, only the ratio. Before patch not recorded 0.149 approx 4× After patch 0.100 0.149 0.67× Repeat 2 — — — Repeat 3 — — — 18 July: the same week, the hollow-fibre set-ups we studied at BIO Asia–Taiwan Did not pass, but we know why A 4× error is an offset, not drift. A loose rail drifts, so it wasn’t the rail. The correction overshoots. We now read under the BioDrop, not over it. One paired reading. Three repeats and a dilution series before this number goes on the wiki. In-line cuvette cannot be cleaned before blanking, and the whole result rests on one pair Add a flush line, then repeat on three separate cultures before we quote the number. Start the long run and see whether it holds calibration on its own.

t: Starting the nineteen-day run
s: Starting the nineteen-day run We had checked the photometer against a benchtop reading once, with someone watching. What we did not know was whether it holds up over days on its own. The reactor was running anyway, so we logged the whole thing from 21 July. PHOTOMETER · LONG RUN · TEST Anton, Noah, Timmy Logged sample and reference illuminance, the ratio, a rejection rate, the point count and elapsed time. Roughly one reading every nine minutes. 20 July: the loop running in the incubator, serum bottle of B. subtilis on the stirrer The photometer column on its wedge inside the chamber Served it on a live dashboard over the local network. Local network only, so nobody can check it from home. There is no alert of any kind, it only draws. Reached 291 points at one day in, with a sample to reference ratio of 7.33. The optics were designed for 10 to 1. We noted the gap and did not explain it. Bubble rejection read zero percent, which we did not question at the time. On other runs it has hit 43 percent. Dashboard at 1 d 6 h 46 m, 291 points: OD600 0.4834, ratio 7.33× 23 July: the curve two days later 21 July: the one-hour mark Left it running instead of tearing it down to chase the ratio. The ratio is a calibration problem we can come back to. The only way to find out whether it survives nineteen days unattended is to leave it alone. TABLE 21 Dashboard reading confirmed independently against the Discord record. Both give 291 points and 7.33×. Points logged 291 — ~1 per 8.9 min Sample channel 195.54 lux — — Reference channel 28.47 lux — — Sample : reference 7.33× 10× unexplained Bubble reject rate 0 % — rule undocumented Let it run instead of stopping to fix the ratio The ratio being off is a calibration question. Whether it survives nineteen days alone is a different one, and the only way to answer it is to leave it running. Tearing it down to chase the 7.33× straight away. We picked the endurance question over the accuracy one and that’s a real trade. Sample to reference sits at 7.33× against a designed 10:1 Measure both channels with the cuvette empty, then blanked, and compare. No pass condition set, and no written bubble rejection rule Decide what counts as holding calibration, and dig the rejection rule out of the firmware. Keep it running. Watch the shape of the curve, not just where it ends up.

t: The photometer catches the pump failing
s: The photometer catches the pump failing The run had been going since 21 July and the curve was not the shape any of us expected. We spent most of the week arguing about why, then on 1 August it dropped and stayed down. PHOTOMETER · PUMP FAILURE · FAILURE DIAGNOSIS Timmy, Noah, Joshua, Chars Nineteen days of continuous logging. No exponential phase at any point, a growth rate that fell away steadily, no plateau, then a rebound part way through. On 1 August the trace dropped sharply and stayed down. Argued about a trace with no exponential phase, a steadily falling growth rate, no plateau, then a rebound. A healthy culture does not do that. We still cannot explain the shape. Guessed contamination when it dropped, that we were watching a second organism take over. That was wrong. We have left it in the record. 3 August: the incubator with the loop, photometer and plants The photometer in the loop at the end of the run The curve on screen, 3 August Found the recirculation pump had failed. Chars confirmed on inspection and replaced it the same evening. Nobody was rostered to check the trace daily, which is why the drop was noticed late. Did not run the flush and reblank that would have separated fouling from biology. Once the run was torn down the chance was gone. 10 d 4 h: rejection 28.6 %, ratio 4.64× shown in red 30 July: the rebound in the curve 3 August: the culture bottle when the loop came apart CANDIDATE CAUSES · TABLE 22 Our first hypothesis was contamination. It was the pump. Recirculation pump failed Inspect the pump. If dead, replace and watch the trace. confirmed Contamination by another organism Plate a sample and look for a different colony morphology. not tested Biowaste accumulation Flush and reblank, then compare against the pre-flush reading. not tested Fouling on the cuvette window Same flush and reblank test distinguishes this from biology. not tested Replace the pump and leave the trace intact The photometer caught a failure in the reactor with nobody watching, which is what we built it to be able to do. The flush-and-reblank test that would have separated fouling from biology. Once the run is torn down you can’t go back, and we didn’t do it. Missing exponential phase unexplained Run plate counts alongside OD next time and check whether OD tracks biomass at all. Flush and reblank never run Do it at the start of the next run, before anything fouls. Plot this trace with the pump-death event annotated. It is the hardware page’s headline figure.

t: Plotting the 434-hour trace with 1 August marked
s: Plotting the 434-hour trace with 1 August marked Entry 22 ended with an action we never closed: plot the long run with the pump failure annotated. This is that plot, made from the raw log (0721, test3 20 day.csv: 2,720 rows, 434.2 hours, 21 July to 8 August). It does not look the way entry 22 describes it, so both are kept. PHOTOMETER · LONG RUN · ANALYSIS from the log Top: OD600 as 2-hour medians of the valid readings. Bottom: the reference channel, which never passes through the culture. The gold band is 1 August, Taiwan time. Plotted the OD in 2-hour medians, and the reference channel underneath it. OD climbs to about 0.94 by 110 h, dips to 0.70 at 145 h, climbs again to a plateau near 1.47 from about 210 h, and declines slowly to 1.07 at the end. That dip and second rise is the ‘rebound’ entry 22 argued about. Found no sharp drop in the OD medians on 1 August. What changes is the light. The reference channel, steady near 26 lux for ten days, drops sharply through 1 August, briefly to single figures, and settles near 22 lux. Around 256 h and again from 281 h individual readings jump by more than 0.3 OD between neighbours, and one reads below zero. The OD is a ratio of sample to reference, so it can hold steady while both channels lose light. A median of that ratio hides the event; the raw lux shows it. Checked it against the Digital Twin analysis, done after the run. Its sensor alarm, trained on the first 120 hours, flagged the photometer at 216.3 h, 26.7 hours before the reading became unusable. Its own table marks 240–434 h as ‘photometer and OD both unreliable’. Report the late part of the run as a sensor failure, not as biology The reference beam never touches the culture, so its collapse is the instrument. Entry 22’s pump failure is still the confirmed event on the bench. What the log adds is that the photometer was losing light at the same time, and the curve after about 240 h cannot be read as growth. Quoting the OD plateau and decline after 240 h as culture behaviour. Nothing in the log separates them from the failing optics. No record of the hour the pump stopped, only the date Log pump state and flow in the same file as OD. Runs 4 to 6 do this. Why both channels lost light is not known Fouling on the cuvette window is the leading guess. The flush and reblank from entry 22 is still the test. Back to August, where the first edition stopped.

t: Decision matrix: pinch valve actuator
s: Decision matrix: pinch valve actuator Prof. Chang told us in June we had no way to push protectant out of the membrane, so we built a stepper pinch valve. This week we replaced it, on criteria written before we scored anything. BIOREACTOR · PINCH VALVE · DECISION Chars, Noah, Anton, Jacquelyn Wrote the criteria first so they could not be bent toward the answer we wanted. Whether it holds when power is cut. Holding force against the permeate pressure. Whether we can build it from parts already in the lab. How much firmware it needs. Scored a stepper, a servo and a solenoid out of five on each. The solenoid is unscored, not zero. We could not source one in time. Chose the servo on the first criterion alone. A stepper lets go when it loses power and the loop is full of live culture. A servo stays tight. Holding on power loss is a safety property, so it outranks the other three. The servo we used is a spare from the VEX kit, not a part chosen for this. 7 August: testing the printed valve parts Tubing through the printed valve body Caught a fit problem by eye before printing anything. The inlet hole needs to be 4 mm and the outlet 6 mm, with tolerance added at CAD. Neither of us has measured what pressure the valve actually needs to hold against. TABLE 23 Scored out of 5 by each of us, then averaged. Row 3 is unscored, not zero. We could not source one in time. Stepper pinch valve 1 4 5 3 13 Servo pinch valve 5 4 4 4 17 Solenoid pinch valve — — — — — Servo pinch valve A stepper lets go when it loses power and the loop is full of live culture, so holding on power loss outranks the other criteria. The stepper we’d already built and knew worked. The effort already spent on it is not a reason to keep it. Scores are ours, not measured Bench-test the holding force and power draw, then rescore rows 2 and 4. Print the servo version with tolerance added and check the fit before committing the CAD.

t: Assembling the full rig
s: Assembling the full rig The valve, the sensors and the photometer had all been built separately. This is the week the whole thing went together as one machine. The ports are not marked on the module, so the orientation has to be remembered. Plumbed the cross-flow loop and wired the electronics. The pump puts a pulse into the flow, and putting the beam after it gives that pulse some line length to smooth out in. 4 August: the perfusion set-up as drawn for the wiki 8 August: the rig set up with the green light for the promotional video The complete rig on the bench Photographed the build across four days without agreeing what to photograph. t: Rewiring the light plate after it stopped lighting
s: Rewiring the light plate after it stopped lighting The packaged LPA had been sitting since July without running a culture. When we came back to it on 7 August, part of the array did not light. This entry was added on 17 October from the photographs and the photo bank; nobody wrote the fault down at the time. LIGHT PLATE · DEBUGGING · WEEK Noah, Anton Opened the LPA and traced the dead channel back through the jumper leads. The harness was still breadboard and jumpers, the open problem from May, and a loose lead is the likeliest cause. The record does not say which lead it was. 7 August: tracing the harness on the open array Lit again on the bench The moment it relit Harness still on jumpers, so a knock can kill a channel Solder the MOSFET stage onto a perfboard inside the housing (done in September, entry 30a). t: Where the bioreactor stood on 13 August
s: Where the bioreactor stood on 13 August This was the last week the first edition of this notebook covered, and the bioreactor was part way through a rebuild with three problems open, all of them mechanical. We had expected the biology to be the hard part. BIOREACTOR · NEXT PHASE · WEEK Anton, Noah, Joshua, Chars Tested the dissolved oxygen and pH probes on the bench on 5 August. Both read in a beaker. Neither had a place in the reservoir yet. 5 August: testing the pH and DO probes Probe readings checked against the meter Wiring the probes to the board Started moving from the peristaltic pump to a magnetic one. A magnetic pump can be driven from the Arduino, which is what lets the system run without someone standing over it. It is weaker and cannot lift liquid out of the serum bottle. Planned a PC-cooler-style clear rectangle with ports top and bottom to get round the head problem. Feed in at the top, draw from the bottom, so gravity does some of the work. It was bought for its shape, not because it is designed for this. Found the dissolved oxygen and pH probes do not fit the reservoir cap. The cap has to be bored out. Keeping it airtight is the harder part, because the sensor body is thicker than its cable and the plug thicker again. Designed a cap in two halves that clamps around the cable and screws shut. Airtight, and nothing gets cut. The first approach was cutting each cable, threading it, and soldering it back. Sketched a sealed cartridge for replenishing B. subtilis, on the printer ink model. It opens only once it is inside the box, so a farmer can top up without a biosafety problem. That creates a second problem. Dead cells clog the loop and block the photometer, so it needs a flush into a waste box. 11 August: changing the hardware CAD on the visit to the 源鮮 hydroponic farm Design around the weak pump instead of reverting Arduino control is the difference between automated and somebody standing there. The peristaltic pump can’t give us that. Going back to the peristaltic pump. It works, and it would cost us the automation this design depends on. (Reversed three days later, entry 24a.) DO and pH probes do not fit the cap Bore the cap out, then print the two-half clamp cap for the cables. No way to clear dead cells from the loop Design the flush and the waste box at the same time as the cartridge. Wet and pressure-test the new membrane, and modify the PC cooler cap so the sensors fit.

t: Pressure on the new membrane, and the magnetic pump fails its first job
s: Pressure on the new membrane, and the magnetic pump fails its first job A new hollow fibre module arrived and had to be wetted and pressure-checked before any culture went into it. The same week the magnetic pump from entry 24 met the loop for the first time. BIOREACTOR · NEW MEMBRANE · TEST Phoebe, Joshua, Chars, Noah Checked what had to be tested before wetting the new module (12 August). Phoebe and Joshua were asked to write the data and the design-build-test-learn steps into the dry lab notebook as they went. Ran the pressure-transducer test on the new module on 13 August, with instructors at the bench. 13 August: pressure-transducer test on the new membrane Reading the transducers on the bench 16 August: the water-cooling reservoir part Noah had taken home to modify Spent 15 August at the whiteboard on what the next reactor chambers should look like. t: Pressure drop against flow rate
s: Pressure drop against flow rate We could read pressure (entry 17) but did not know what pressure the module should show at a given flow. Without that baseline, a rise from fouling and a rise from simply pumping faster look the same. Pass condition: measured pressure drop agrees with Hagen–Poiseuille theory for our fibre geometry over the range we would run. BIOREACTOR · HYDRAULICS · TEST Chars, Noah Logged pressure against flow on 16 August with the transducers and the flow meter. Chars posted the spreadsheet (260816_pressure_to_flow_rate.xlsx) and an analysis on 18 August. Fitted net module pressure drop, background subtracted, to ΔP = aQ + bQ² through the origin. From 113 to 263 mL/min the measured points sit at 0.90 to 0.96 times the Hagen–Poiseuille prediction. Above 300 mL/min they diverge to 1.26 times, as minor losses at the headers grow. Checked the fibre geometry two independent ways. Wall shear rate computed from flow and geometry, and from the measured pressure drop, agree within 10 % across the safe range. That confirms the assumed fibre count and bore. Net module pressure drop against cross-flow rate (Noah’s draft figure, 5 September). Star: chosen operating point, 263 mL/min at TMP 0.30 bar. n = 1 per point. Picked 263 mL/min as the operating point, with a ceiling at 300 mL/min. Passed below 300 mL/min. Run at 263 mL/min Measured and theoretical pressure drop agree within 10 % up to 263 mL/min. Above 300 mL/min the header losses take over, so that is the ceiling. One point per flow rate. And see the problem below: the absolute pressures were later found to be scaled wrongly in the firmware. Every logged pressure is out by 4.8× The firmware scaled the 0–1 MPa transducer as 0–30 psi. Rescale this data set before quoting the TMP at the operating point, and recheck the ratio to theory. n = 1 at every flow rate Repeat the sweep, up and down in flow, on a clean module. Move the whole loop into one enclosure.

t: Rebuilding the reactor inside a computer case

t: Calibrating against weighed titanium dioxide
s: Calibrating against weighed titanium dioxide Entries 16 and 20 left two open problems: we did not know if the response was linear, and we had one paired reading against the BioDrop. A growing culture changes while it is measured, so we needed an inert standard added in weighed steps. Pass condition: both instruments linear against mass, and the raw photometer within 10 % of the BioDrop. PHOTOMETER · TiO₂ CALIBRATION · TEST Noah, Joshua, Anton, Chars Suspended TiO₂ in 500 mL of 1 % SDS and circulated it through the loop past the photometer. The iGEM protocol specifies silica. TiO₂ was on hand and behaved almost identically in SDS. 15 August: preparing the calibration run About to start 23 August: reading the BioDrop alongside the photometer, instructors watching Ran two series, each step read on the BioDrop and the photometer. Test 1: 1 mg per step, 40 points. Test 2: 1 mg per step to 10 mg, then 5 mg per step to 60 mg. Got both instruments linear against mass, and the raw photometer close to the BioDrop. Both regress against TiO₂ mass with R² > 0.999. The raw, uncalibrated output tracked the BioDrop with a median paired difference of 3.8 %. Test 2’s raw points scatter about the line of identity with an RMSE of 0.011 OD600 (R² = 0.9997). Test 2: OD600 of both instruments against TiO₂ added Test 2: raw photometer against BioDrop, with the line of identity Excluded two single BioDrop points and kept both in the plot as open markers. 37 mg in Test 1 and 5 mg in Test 2 each sat off the trend of their neighbours while the paired photometer reading stayed on trend, which puts the error in the reference. Passed. No correction transform applied 3.8 % median difference against a 10 % target, with no calibration fitted. Fitting our readings to the BioDrop would only tie them to the BioDrop’s own error. Neither TiO₂ series went above OD600 1.9, and TiO₂ does not scatter exactly like bacteria. Top of the range untested Run silica, the iGEM standard, further up (done 10 October, entry 33a). A mineral standard is not a culture Repeat with B. subtilis at known cell densities before quoting cell numbers. Back to the case. Five September is a public forum.

t: First integrated run: the protectant crosses the membrane
s: First integrated run: the protectant crosses the membrane Every piece had been tested alone. The loop ran for days with OD, flow and pressure logged and nobody drawing a sample. The band is faint and no concentration or transfer rate was measured. The pressure transducers had no filters on this build, so their readings could not be calibrated (Chars, 15 September). Protectant transfer rate unmeasured Measure shell-side concentration over time.
